ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Data collection of the Stress and Personality Assessment (SPA) Study was approved by local ethics committee of University of Zurich [Protocol number: 24.08.22] and data were collected in accordance with the 2024 version of the Declaration of Helsinki.
After registration, participants were directed to the baseline survey (T1) which included questions about trait-level personal characteristics (e.g., neuroticism, depression).
After receiving a prompt, participants had 60 minutes to complete the survey.
Every night (at 9pm), participants were invited to a daily-diary assessment.
Participants had 180 minutes to respond to this prompt.

Furthermore, participants completed a checklist of major life stressors, provided information on the timing of all experienced events, and identified the most important major life stressor they had experienced in the last month (i.e., since the start of the study).

We preregistered to exclude data from these assessments if participants completed a survey in less than 1 minute and additionally responded to more than 80% of the items for personality traits, reassurance seeking, depression, and rumination with the same response; however, no participant had to be excluded based on this criterion.
On average, participants completed 44.46 ESM surveys (nobservations = 18,360) and 9.61 daily dairies (nobservations = 3,727).
Participants were on average 26.86 years old (SD = 8.99); 69% of the sample were female and 93% of the sample reported having at least a high school diploma.
Participants were primarily German (55%) or Swiss (27%).

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: SPA-Study
table.description:
The SPA-Study will employ an experience sampling design, comprising two trait assessments and a 2-week experience sampling phase. The study will be addressed to the general public and data will be collected using formR UZH (https://formr-admin.psych.uzh.ch). 
The overall goal of the SPA-Study will be to provide a better understanding of stress generation processes in daily life. Stress generation refers to the phenomenon that individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of stressful events in their lives (Hammen, 1991, 2006). Existing stress generation research has shown that personal characteristics like personality traits predict the occurrence of major life stressors several months or years later (Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023). However, less is known about the process of stress generation on shorter time scales in daily life, that is, how momentary personal characteristics predict the occurrence of minor stressors (also called daily hassles). Data from the SPA-Study will be used to examine how different momentary personal characteristics predict the occurrence of daily hassles and to explore possible mechanisms of these effects.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. **Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. **`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

text.text: Stress generation describes that people with mental health problems actively contribute to the occurrence of stressful events in their lives, which can lead to detrimental cycles between stress and mental health.
However, existing research has focused on long-term stress generation.
Here, we aimed to advance the understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales by combing experience sampling, daily diary, and 1-month longitudinal data (N = 403).

We found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were linked to the occurrence of daily hassles over hours and days and major life stressors over a month.
Furthermore, momentary neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of daily hassles over several hours.
Finally, some indicators of hourly and daily stress generation prospectively predicted the occurrence of major life stressors.
These findings provide the starting point for a thorough understanding of how stress generation unfolds over time.

Stressful events, such as relationship conflicts, job loss, or divorce, have been linked to a broad range of detrimental outcomes, including the onset of mental disorders, physical health problems, and decreases in well-being (Asselmann et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2019; DeLongis et al., 1982; Haehner, Fliedner, et al., 2024; Luhmann et al., 2012).

text.text: With the present study, we aimed to better understand how stress generation processes unfold across different timescales.

In contrast, independent stressful events (e.g., death of a loved one) are theorized to be relatively independent of a person's influence.
The Stress Generation Hypothesis posits that depressed people behave in a way that leads to the occurrence of dependent but not independent stressful events.

text.text: There are, however, several limitations of existing research on short-term stress generation that impede a comprehensive understanding of the temporal unfolding of these processes.

First, most studies did not examine whether state-level personal characteristics prospectively predict the occurrence of dependent daily hassles, providing limited insight into the temporal direction of person-hassle transactions (Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Shih & Auerbach, 2010; but see Conway et al., 2024).

text.text: Second, only a few studies moved beyond daily assessment intervals (i.e., incorporated multiple assessments per day), so the question of whether stress generation unfolds across even shorter timescales still needs to be addressed (but see Conway et al., 2024; Sears et al., 2018; Vize et al., 2024).

text.text: Third, existing research has not yet compared stress generation processes across different timescales, thereby providing little insight into how stress generation effects may diverge or converge across time intervals.

Thus, the first goal of the present study was to examine whether established predictors of stress generation-depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism-predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events over hours, days, and one month.
Examining stress generation across different timescales also enables an examination of how short-and long-term stress generation processes are related to each other.

In line with theories on person-environment transactions, Haehner, Andrae, et al. (2026) hypothesized that short-term stress generation processes are the building blocks of long-term stress generation.

text.text: For example, behaving more neurotic than usual in a given moment may lead to the experience of a dependent daily hassle like a relationship conflict.

Over time, these within-person effects may accumulate and explain the between-person and long-term longitudinal link between trait neuroticism and dependent major life stressors (e.g., ongoing relationship conflicts causing a breakup).

However, this hypothesis has not yet been empirically tested and other researchers have posited that the generation of dependent daily hassles and dependent major life stressors may be relatively independent of each other.

For instance, Starr et al. (2025) suggested that although "hassle generation" may be a clinically relevant form of stress generation in its own regard, it may not necessarily be related to the generation of major life stressors, because many hassles that are stressful in the short-term result in desirable outcomes in the long run (e.g., dealing with relationship conflicts could even lead to a more resilient relationship).

text.text: To evaluate these conflicting views, a second goal of the present study was to examine whether stress generation over hours or days predicts stress generation processes occurring over one month.
The goal of the present study was to better understand the temporal unfolding of stress generation processes.

We examined links between four established risk factors of stress generation-depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism-and the occurrence of dependent stressful events across three timescales: hours using experience sampling data, days using daily-diary data, and one month using longitudinal surveys.

The hourly and daily timescales captured short-term stress generation processes with daily hassles as the dependent variable whereas the monthly timescale was used to capture longer-term stress generation processes with major life stressors as the dependent variable.
We addressed two research questions: (1) Which personal characteristics predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events across hours, days, and one month?
(2) Do stress generation processes over hours and days predict stress generation over the course of one month?

Furthermore, we also explored these same research questions for independent stressful events to probe the distinction between dependent and independent events emphasized by the Stress Generation Hypothesis.

Based on existing evidence on short-and long-term stress generation, we tested six confirmatory hypotheses: Depression and neuroticism predict the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over days (Hypotheses 1 and 2), and depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predict the occurrence of major life stressors over one month (Hypotheses 3 to 6).

text.text: Data collection of the Stress and Personality Assessment (SPA) Study was approved by local ethics committee of University of Zurich [Protocol number: 24.08.22] and data were collected in accordance with the 2024 version of the Declaration of Helsinki.
The SPA Study consisted of two survey assessments one month apart with a 2-week experience sampling phase in between.
Data were collected using formR (Arslan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Data were collected using formR <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arslan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Participants interested in the SPA Study first had to complete a registration form and provide informed consent.
After registration, participants were directed to the baseline survey (T1) which included questions about trait-level personal characteristics (e.g., neuroticism, depression).
Furthermore, participants could pick an individual start date for the experience sampling phase within 2 weeks after the baseline assessment.
During the 2-week experience sampling phase, participants received email invitations for six experience sampling method (ESM) surveys and one daily-diary survey per day.

The ESM surveys were pseudo-randomly distributed throughout the day, with assessments being prompted during the following intervals: (1) 9am -9:45 am, (2) 11am -11:45 pm, (3) 1pm -1:45pm, (4) 3pm -3:45pm, (5) 5pm -5:45pm, (6) 7pm -7:45pm.
After receiving a prompt, participants had 60 minutes to complete the survey.

In the ESM surveys, participants rated their momentary personal characteristics (e.g., momentary rumination) and were asked whether they had experienced a daily hassle since the last assessment and, if yes, provided details on the event occurrence.
Every night (at 9pm), participants were invited to a daily-diary assessment.
Participants had 180 minutes to respond to this prompt.
In the daily-diary assessments, participants reported on their thoughts, feelings, and behaviors throughout the day.
Furthermore, participants received a checklist of daily hassles, provided information on the timing of all experienced hassles, and identified the most important hassle of each day.
After the experience sampling phase, there was a break of up to 2 weeks-depending on participants' individualized start date.
The post assessment (T2) then comprised questions about participants' trait-level personal characteristics, similar to the baseline assessment.

Furthermore, participants completed a checklist of major life stressors, provided information on the timing of all experienced events, and identified the most important major life stressor they had experienced in the last month (i.e., since the start of the study).

text.text: The SPA Study included German speaking adults (minimum age: 18 years).
Recruitment addressed people who frequently feel stressed.
Participants could receive up to CHF 30 for taking part in the study with compensation being contingent on the completion of the surveys.
Furthermore, participants could receive partial course credit and feedback on their Big Five personality trait profile.
Overall, 591 people registered to take part in the SPA Study.
However, for the present study, only participants who started the phase of intensive longitudinal assessments were considered (n = 414).

Furthermore, we excluded data from the baseline and post assessments (n = 11) if a participant failed to respond correctly to one or more instructed response items (e.g., "To ensure data quality, please select the response option 3").
Additionally, for the ESM and daily-diary assessments, we checked for careless responding using the longstring indicator from the careless package (Yentes & Wilhelm, 2023).

Applying these exclusion criteria led to a final sample size of N = 403.
On average, participants completed 44.46 ESM surveys (nobservations = 18,360) and 9.61 daily dairies (nobservations = 3,727).
Participants were on average 26.86 years old (SD = 8.99); 69% of the sample were female and 93% of the sample reported having at least a high school diploma.
Participants were primarily German (55%) or Swiss (27%).

At the daily timescale (daily-diary assessments), participants received a checklist of daily hassles and checked all events they had experienced on that day.

This checklist was based on existing approaches (Cummings et al., 2010; Sahl et al., 2009) and we categorized hassles as dependent (failed to reach a personal goal at work, university or school; received negative feedback on my performance at work, university or school; failed to reach a daily fitness goal; did something embarrassing in a social situation; argument or conflict with partner or family members; argument or conflict with friend or other close person; argument or conflict with a stranger; been hurt, rejected or criticized by a close person) or independent (illness or injury; mobility-related problem; victim of crime; technical problems).

To facilitate the interpretation of effects, we standardized all personal characteristics using their grand mean and grand standard deviation at their respective timescale.
For example, we standardized ESM depression using the mean and standard deviation of all ESM depression ratings.
Using this approach, all effects have a comparable metric across constructs and timescales (i.e., timescale specific standard deviation units).
To examine hourly stress generation, we used logistic multilevel models with assessments (j) nested in participants (i).
The occurrence of dependent daily hassles since the last assessment served as binary dependent variable (0 = no,1 = yes).

The person-mean of a personal characteristic (e.g., person-mean of depression) and the person-mean centered personal characteristic at the previous assessment (e.g., person-mean centered depression at j -1) served as predictors to examine between-person effects and lagged within-person effects, respectively.
Furthermore, we controlled for the time interval between assessments (standardized), whether assessments occurred on weekends versus weekdays, and gender (dichotomized).
An example model equation reads as follows: We used a similar analysis strategy to examine daily stress generation.
The main difference was that we used the number of experienced dependent daily hassles on a certain day as dependent variable as opposed to the binary hassle indicator.
Consequently, we used Poisson multilevel models instead of logistic multilevel models to model this count variable.
To increase interpretability of effects, we transformed fixed effects to incidence rate ratios (IRR) and count differences (CD).
CD describe the absolute difference in the number of expected events between people with different levels of the predictor (e.g., +1 SD vs. -1 SD of depressive symptoms).
Finally, to examine monthly stress generation, we moved from a multilevel modeling framework to single-level Poisson regression models.

In these models, we did not distinguish between-person and within-person effects (as is typical in long-term stress generation research), but we used the personal characteristics assessed at baseline as predictors of the number of dependent major life stressors reported at post assessment, thus establishing temporal precedence of the predictors.
We again included gender and time (but not weekday) as covariates and transformed effects to IRR and CD to increase interpretability.
For Research Question 2, we were interested in whether and how stress generation processes across different timescales interacted with each other.
We examined two processes predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors across the study period.

The interaction effects (b5, b6, and b7) indicate whether monthly stress generation effects (i.e., the association between the baseline personal characteristic and the number of dependent major life stressors) depended on aggregated characteristics of the hourly stress generation processes.
A significant positive interaction effect would indicate that stress generation processes in daily life amplify long-term stress generation effects.
To increase interpretability, we again transformed coefficients to IRR.
To examine the interplay of daily and monthly stress generation, we repeated these analyses using data assessed in the daily diaries and random effects from the stress-generationover-days model.
We again examined main effects and the interaction effects of the daily stress generation indicators to evaluate the interplay of daily and monthly stress generation effects.
To examine the specificity of stress generation effects for dependent stressful events, we repeated all analyses using independent stressful events as criterion variables.
This allowed us to compare effect sizes for the generation of dependent and independent stressful events and thus provided a more stringent test of the Stress Generation Hypothesis (Hammen, 1991).

Events Across Hours, Days, or Weeks?
As a first step, we examined whether depressive symptoms, rumination, reassurance seeking, and depression predicted the occurrence of dependent stressful events across hours, days, and one month.
The results of these analyses are illustrated in Figure 1 and summarized in Table 2.

text.text: Overall, we found robust evidence for between-person effects across all timescales.
That is, higher average levels of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination consistently predicted the occurrence of a higher number of dependent stressful events.

Effect sizes ranged from OR = 1.28 to OR = 1.74 across hours, from IRR = 1.28 to IRR = 1.58 across days, and from IRR = 1.19 to IRR = 1.34 across one month, indicating small between-person associations (Chen et al., 2010; Funder & Ozer, 2019).
text.formatted: Effect sizes ranged from OR = 1.28 to OR = 1.74 across hours, from IRR = 1.28 to IRR = 1.58 across days, and from IRR = 1.19 to IRR = 1.34 across one month, indicating small between-person associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chen et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Funder & Ozer, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, a person with above average levels (+ 1 SD) of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination has a 0.02 to 0.03 point higher probability to experience a hassle at the hourly timescale, experiences 0.12 to 0.25 more hassles more at the daily timescale, and 0.08 to 0.14 more hassles at the monthly timescale than a person with average levels.
Evidence for within-person effects was less consistent.

Within-person increases in rumination (OR = 1.16) and neuroticism (OR = 1.19) prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles at the hourly timescale, but no other within-person effect reached statistical significance.

Thus, our findings were in line with Hypotheses 3 to 6 (depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predict dependent stressful events over one month) and partly in line with Hypotheses 1 and 2 (depression and neuroticism predict stressful events over days) as we only found significant between-person effects.

As people reported relatively few dependent stressful events across the study period, we repeated the analyses of the daily and monthly stress generation model, using logistic instead of Poisson regressions by dichotomizing the dependent variable (0 = no dependent stressful experienced,1 = at least one dependent stressful event experienced).

All significant effects from our main analysis replicated in this robustness check, supporting the robustness of findings across the two analysis approaches (see Section 2 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f for details).

text.text: In a second step, we examined whether stress generation processes observed at shorter timescales could predict stress generation processes on longer timescales.
The findings from these analyses are illustrated in Figures 2 and 3.
text.formatted: The findings from these analyses are illustrated in Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>.

text.text: Adding indicators from the hourly stress generation model to the monthly model, we found that a higher number of dependent daily hassles at the hourly level predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment in two of the four models (reassurance seeking: IRR = 1.29, p = .004; neuroticism: IRR = 1.27, p = .042).
These findings indicate that people who experience more dependent hassles at the hourly timescale also tend to report a higher number of major life stressors at post assessment.

Furthermore, higher average ratings of depressive symptoms (IRR = 1.78, p = .001) and rumination (IRR = 1.39, p = .011) during the ESM surveys predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment, suggesting that these average momentary ratings of depression and rumination predict the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment beyond people's baseline levels of these traits.
Finally, there was only one interaction effect between indicators of hourly stress generation and people's baseline characteristics and this effect was in an unexpected direction.

People who reported a higher number of dependent hassles in the ESM surveys had weaker links between reassurance seeking at baseline and the occurrence of dependent major life stressors (IRR = 0.67, p = .001).
Two of these effects were replicated when adding indicators from the daily stress generation model to the monthly model.

Specifically, higher levels of depressive symptoms (IRR = 1.60, p = .003) and rumination (IRR = 1.38, p = .031) during the daily diaries predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment, supporting that momentary ratings of these constructs have predictive value for the occurrence of major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline levels of these traits.
Furthermore, we found a positive interaction between people's baseline levels of neuroticism and the number of reported dependent hassles on dependent major life stressors (IRR = 1.54, p = .048).
This effect indicates that people who experience more daily hassles have stronger links between their baseline neuroticism and the number of reported dependent major life stressors.

However, the findings from these crosstimescale analyses should be interpreted with caution because we found that the person-specific slopes (SGhours and SGdays) that we extracted from the hourly and daily stress generation models had a low reliability (hourly: .05 to .49; daily: .58 to .60).
Thus, the lack of cross-timescale interactions may at least partly be explained by the limited precession to capture these effects in our sample.

With the present study, we aimed to advance our understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales.

Using hourly, daily, and monthly data, we found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were robustly linked to the occurrence of dependent stressful events across all three timescales.

A person with above average levels of depressive symptoms, neuroticism, reassurance seeking, and rumination has a 0.02 to 0.03 point higher probability to experience a hassle at the hourly timescale, experiences 0.12 to 0.25 more hassles more at the daily timescale, and 0.08 to 0.14 more hassles at the monthly timescale.

Furthermore, within-person increases in neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles at the next assessment, providing insights into the mechanisms of stress generation in daily life.

Crosstimescale analyses showed that the occurrence of dependent daily hassles and average momentary depression and rumination ratings predicted the occurrence of major life stressors over one month, illustrating their utility to predict long-term stress generation effects above and beyond baseline levels of these traits.

In contrast, we found limited evidence for interactions of stress generation processes across timescales, which could partly be explained by methodological problems to capture these interactions, outlining the necessity for future crosstemporal research.
In the following, we discuss the insights of our study for short-term stress generation and the interplay of stress generation process across timescales.

Stress generation research has traditionally focused on longer-term longitudinal links between personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several weeks, months, or years (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Stress generation research has traditionally focused on longer-term longitudinal links between personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several weeks, months, or years <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Rnic et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Santee et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In line with the existing evidence on this topic, we found that people with higher levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism reported a higher number of dependent major life stressors a month later.
Moving beyond the monthly level, we replicated these between-person associations at hourly and daily timescales.

These effects indicate that people with higher average levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism in daily life experience more dependent daily hassles than people with lower average levels of these risk factors.

These results confirm and extend the initial evidence on stress generation, showing that depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism are important risk factors for the occurrence of dependent daily hassles and major life stressors across different timescales (Cummings et al., 2010; Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Sahl et al., 2009; Shih & Auerbach, 2010).

text.text: Interestingly, between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism predicted both dependent and independent stressful events.
Relatedly, correlations between personal characteristics and daily hassles were of similar size for dependent versus independent events (see Section 1 of the https://osf.io/pcjnb/files/qkx9f).

text.text: These results are at odds with the Stress Generation Hypothesis but matches existing meta-analytic findings (Hammen, 1991; R. T. Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: The Stress Generation Hypothesis states that people with certain risk factors should only differ in the experience of dependent stressful events, because they behave in a way that makes those events more likely.
In contrast, independent stressful events are, by definition, out of a person's control.
One explanation for why predictive effects for independent events may have emerged is reporting bias (Hammen, 2006; Monroe, 2008).
text.formatted: One explanation for why predictive effects for independent events may have emerged is reporting bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hammen, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Monroe, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: People with higher levels of depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism may experience events as more stressful and thus be more likely to report these events as hassles (Haehner et al., 2023; Wenzel et al., 2025).

text.text: Designs that can separate the occurrence and the appraisal of events would be necessary to test this explanation (see Limitations section for details).
An alternative explanation is that the dichotomous distinction between dependent and independent stressful events is imperfect.
Almost no event is entirely independent of the person (Kandler et al., 2012; Plomin & Bergeman, 1991).
text.formatted: Almost no event is entirely independent of the person <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kandler et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Plomin & Bergeman, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: For example, technical and mobility-related problems were classified as independent daily hassles in the present study.
However, one can easily imagine scenarios where these events actually depend on the behavior of a person (e.g., a computer crash because a person forgot to update their computer).

An important direction for future research would thus be to move beyond the simplistic distinction of dependent and independent events and instead consider a broader range of relevant event characteristics that may help to understand which kinds of events people experience in which contexts (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Starr et al., 2025).

text.text: We also examined whether state-level personal characteristics prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles (i.e., a prospective within-person effect).

We found two within-person effects at the hourly timescale: Higher momentary levels of neuroticism and rumination relative to one's average predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over several hours.

These effects could indicate that being neurotic or ruminating in a given moment binds people's resources, which in turn could make the occurrence of dependent hassles like failing at a work-related task or being late to a meeting more likely.
In line with the Stress Generation Hypothesis, these within-person effects were more consistent for dependent than for independent daily hassles.

These results are similar to those reported by Sahl et al. (2009) and Conway et al. (2024) who found that hostility and a sense of urgency prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles.
text.formatted: These results are similar to those reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Sahl et al. (2009)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Conway et al. (2024)</ref> who found that hostility and a sense of urgency prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles.

text.text: Together, these findings on within-person predictors of dependent daily hassles could provide initial insights into stress generation from a mechanistic perspective by drawing attention to how individuals generate stress (Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Together, these findings on within-person predictors of dependent daily hassles could provide initial insights into stress generation from a mechanistic perspective by drawing attention to how individuals generate stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Eberhart & Hammen, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, experimental approaches would be needed that manipulate state-level predictors of stress generation (e.g., temporary increase or decrease rumination) to fully understand stress generation mechanisms and to test the causal relevance of the identified within-person effects.

In summary, the present study shows that between-person associations among depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism with dependent daily hassles and major life stressors can be observed over hours, days, and one month.
However, these effects may partly be inflated due to reporting bias or ambiguous distinctions between event types as we found similar associations for independent events.

At the within-person level, being neurotic or ruminating in a given moment prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles, providing initial insights into the mechanisms of stress generation in daily life.

In addition to examining stress generation over hours, days, and one month, the present study aimed to better understand whether and how stress generation processes interact across relatively independently of each other, meaning that the processes that lead to the generation of daily hassles differ from those that lead to the occurrence of major life stressors.
Overall, we found limited evidence for interactions between short-and long-term stress generation processes, rather supporting the view of Starr and colleagues.
However, there are some caveats to this conclusion.
First, there were some main effects of indicators of short-term stress generation predicting the occurrence of major life stressors at post assessment.

For example, higher average levels of depression and rumination in the ESM surveys and daily diaries predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline levels of depression and rumination.
Similarly, the occurrence of dependent hassles in daily life predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors at post assessment.

Thus, even if short-term stress generation processes do not modulate long-term stress generation effects, indicators of short-term stress generation still improved the prediction of who experienced dependent major life stressors.

This finding could thus be of practical relevance to design interventions to reduce stress generation, because it suggests that momentary expressions of rumination and depression would be suitable intervention targets (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026).

text.text: For example, just-in-time adaptive interventions that target high statelevels of depression and rumination could serve a double purpose by reducing short-term stress generation processes and helping reduce people's trait levels of depression and neuroticism over time (Nahum-Shani et al., 2015).

text.text: Second, our analyses showed that investigating stress generation effects across timescales is challenging.
Even though we had a relatively large number of observations (Nobs = 18,360), the person-specific slopes extracted from the daily and hourly stress generation models had a low reliability.
Thus, the limited evidence for interactions across timescales could at least partly be explained by a lack of precision to identify these effects.

However, beyond increasing the number of observations, the precision of these within-person slopes also depends on factors that are hard to control such as the within-person variance of predictors (S. Liu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, beyond increasing the number of observations, the precision of these within-person slopes also depends on factors that are hard to control such as the within-person variance of predictors (S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Liu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Methodological advancements that can account for measurement error in these personspecific may help addressing this problem in the future (Lai & Liu, 2026).
text.formatted: Methodological advancements that can account for measurement error in these personspecific may help addressing this problem in the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lai & Liu, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A critical goal for future research would also be to further disentangle which stress generation predictors operate at which timescale to develop an integrative theoretical model.

Ideally, we would have specific hypotheses on how between-person differences in stable risk factors are related to within-person increases in relevant states that then lead to the occurrence of daily hassles and major life stressors.

For example, neuroticism may best be conceptualized as a predictor of long-term stress generation whereas specific behaviors (e.g., a flippant reaction, a clingy behavior) may be the active ingredients of short-term stress generation.
Different assessment methods could help to clearly distinguish these predictors (e.g., self-report versus behavioral observation).
Furthermore, future research should investigate the types of daily hassles more thoroughly.
In the present study, we considered the overall sum of experienced daily hassles and people's overall state-level-hassle links as predictors of major life stressors.
However, it could be the case that interactions between short-and long-term stress generation are domain-specific.
For example, the accumulation of relationship conflicts may predict the occurrence of interpersonal major life stressors but not work-related major life stressors.

Overall, the present study should thus be seen as a starting point to better understand the interplay of stress generation processes across timescales, hopefully inspiring future research on this topic.

The present study has several limitations.
First, our sample was highly educated, predominantly female, and recruited in German-speaking Western countries.

As stress generation research has primarily been conducted in the United States (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023), the findings of the present study can help to understand whether stress generation processes generalize across different Western contexts.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether findings generalize to individuals from other socioeconomic or cultural backgrounds (R. T. Liu et al., 2024).

text.text: Second, participants reported relatively few stressful event occurrences across the study period.

Although the number of event occurrences seems to be comparable those reported in existing research (e.g., Almeida et al., 2023), larger effects for stress generation may be observed in clinical samples, which tend to experience stressful events more frequently (Rnic et al., 2023).

text.text: However, in particular, for the monthly timescale, for which we assessed major life stressors, a low base rate can generally be expected.
Third, we examined stress generation over one month to represent long-term stress generation.

Although a time interval of one month could be a reasonable starting point when aiming to connect short-and long-term perspectives on stress generation, one month rather represents the lower bound for examining stress generation, with existing research mostly using time intervals of several months or years (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: Fourth, the measures to assess depression, rumination, and reassurance seeking slightly differed across timescales.
For example, we used fewer items to assess constructs in the ESM surveys and daily diaries.

Assessing constructs like depression or neuroticism with few items may limit reliability and content validity (Rammstedt & Beierlein, 2014), which in turn could restrict power to identify significant effects.
text.formatted: Assessing constructs like depression or neuroticism with few items may limit reliability and content validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rammstedt & Beierlein, 2014)</ref>, which in turn could restrict power to identify significant effects.

text.text: On the other hand, the higher number of ESM surveys compared to daily diaries increased power at the hourly timescale, which could explain why we only found within-person effects for the hourly timescale.
Fifth, in the present study, we did not use interview methods to capture the occurrence of stressful events.

Interview methods are advantageous to assess the occurrence of stressful events because they may help disentangle stressor occurrence and personal characteristics (Hammen, 2006; Harkness & Monroe, 2016; Monroe, 2008; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: However, due to their high burden for researchers and participants, interview methods are more difficult to be integrated in intensive longitudinal studies (Starr et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, due to their high burden for researchers and participants, interview methods are more difficult to be integrated in intensive longitudinal studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Starr et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The reliance on self-report measures across timescales to assess both stressor occurrence and personal characteristics may have inflated associations in our study.
Future research using interview methods may also help to more accurately distinguish between independent and dependent events.

Sixth, when examining stress generation processes across timescales, we used a twostep approach using indicators of short-term stress generation from the hourly and daily multilevel models as predictors of major life stressors in separate regressions.

While alternative approaches could not directly be applied to our research question (e.g., MSEMs), this two-step approach is limited by the low reliability of the extracted effects (S. Liu et al., 2021).

text.text: Future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to better understand possible interactions between short-and long-term stress generation.

Studies with an even larger number of observations per person and methodological advancements that can account for unreliability of the two-step approach may help to address this problem in the future.

Large-scale longitudinal studies and comprehensive meta-analyses have shown that personal characteristics predict the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several months and years, while the links between personal characteristics and dependent daily hassles over the course of hours and days have received comparatively less research attention (Haehner, Andrae, et al., 2026; R. T. Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: Examining stress generation over hours, days, and one month, we found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism are linked to the occurrence of dependent stressful events over hours, days, and one month, indicating that similar individual differences contribute to the generation of dependent daily hassles and major life stressor across different timescales.

Furthermore, being neurotic and ruminating in a given moment prospectively predicted the occurrence of dependent daily hassles over several hours, pointing to a potential mechanism of stress generation in daily life.

Finally, some indicators of shortterm stress generation-averaged state-level characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles-predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over one month.
These findings provide a useful foundation for a more thorough empirical investigation and theoretical integration of how stress generation unfolds over time.

To examine the interplay of hourly and monthly stress generation, we first obtained person-level slopes (i.e., empirical Bayes estimates) from the hourly stress generation models from Research Question 1.
These person-specific slopes capture between-person differences in the link between momentary personal characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles (henceforward called SGHours).

Then, we added SGHours, the person-mean of the personal characteristics assessed in the ESM surveys (Person.mean), and each person's average number of experienced dependent stressful events during the ESM period (Event.avg) to the monthly stress generation model from Research Question 1.
Furthermore, we included interactions between the baseline personal characteristic (PersBaseline) and SGHours, Person.mean, and Event.avg.

Drawing on theories on person-environment transactions, Haehner, Andrae, et al. (2026) posited that short-term stress generation processes are the building blocks of long-term stress generation effects, implying that indicators of short-term stress generation should be able to predict long-term stress generation effects.

In contrast, Starr et al. (2025) posited that short-and long-term stress generation processes likely operate people's average levels of state-level characteristics and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles-predicted the occurrence of dependent major life stressors above and beyond people's baseline personal characteristics.
These findings are an important first step towards a more comprehensive understanding of how stress generation processes unfold across different timescales.
Future research on this topic is warranted, because it connects established findings of between-person effects on stress generation to its within-person mechanisms.

This evidence is crucial to design effective interventions against stress generation because it helps to identify people at risk for stress generation (i.e., between-person effects) while also elucidating when and how individuals generate stress (i.e., within-person effects).
